video_notes.title: Building beautiful UI using AI (My design workflow)
video_notes.contributed: A concrete, repeatable workflow for generating a consistent design system and tokens with AI (Claude Design) and porting it into an AI coding agent (Claude Code) so every generated page matches.

claims.claim: Pick among five rendering strategies before anything else: static site generation (fastest, pre-built), incremental static regeneration (updates static pages without full rebuild), server-side rendering (dynamic content per request), client-side rendering (blank HTML then fetch/compile), and partial pre-rendering (mixes pre-rendered and dynamic).
claims.quote: five main different strategies that we can use

claims.claim: As a front end grows and deploys get riskier, split it into independently deployable micro-frontends, each free to choose its own rendering strategy (e.g. SSG for product pages, SSR for checkout, CSR for chat).
claims.quote: splitting the application into independent and Deployable pieces

claims.claim: Module Federation on Webpack 5 is the key tool for dynamically loading separate micro-frontend applications into one page.
claims.quote: module federations using webpack 5 which dynamically loads different micr and applications

claims.claim: Use Chrome DevTools' Performance tab to track First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive before optimizing anything, so you fix the actual bottleneck.
claims.quote: track the first contentful paint and time to interactive

claims.claim: In React, a parent re-render cascades to all children by default; wrap components in React.memo so they only re-render when their props actually change.
claims.quote: memorize the component so that it only rerenders if the props change

claims.claim: Use useCallback to memoize functions passed to children so they aren't recreated (and don't trigger child re-renders) on every parent render.
claims.quote: memorize the functions to prevent the unnecessary function Recreations

claims.claim: Use useMemo to cache expensive calculations so they aren't recomputed on every render.
claims.quote: cach the expensive calculations of a function to avoid recompute

claims.claim: Lazy-load heavy components (e.g. dashboard charts/analytics) only when the user actually triggers them, instead of loading everything up front, to shrink the initial bundle and speed perceived load.
claims.quote: instead of loading everything up front we can choose to load components when the user needs them

claims.claim: Reduce JS bundle size with tree shaking to strip unused code and split bundles so pages load faster.
claims.quote: tree shakings to remove the unus code and split bundles

claims.claim: Cache server responses in client-side state management so repeat reads (e.g. a training list re-shown after an add/delete) don't require a fresh GET request every time.
claims.quote: we can be able to use State Management to reduce the number of calls

claims.claim: Client-side caches can go stale when other users mutate the same data elsewhere; mitigate by setting an expiration so the cache is periodically refreshed.
claims.quote: maybe by setting an expiration on our cache so maybe after a certain period of time we're going to refresh the data

claims.claim: React Query's useQuery lets you set a staleTime so a cached, non-expired response is reused instead of re-hitting the API.
claims.quote: setting a stale time which is a expiration on when we're going to make another call to the API

claims.claim: Use GraphQL to request only the fields the UI actually needs (e.g. name and price, not the full product record) instead of overfetching a full REST payload.
claims.quote: use tools like graphql to be able to reduce the over fashion data

claims.claim: Apollo Client supports in-memory caching, so a repeated query for the same record (e.g. book ID 5) is served from cache instead of hitting the server again.
claims.quote: aollo client also supports in memory caching as well

claims.claim: Debounce search inputs (e.g. 500ms via lodash) so the app waits until the user stops typing before calling the API, instead of firing a request per keystroke.
claims.quote: wait 500 milliseconds after user stop typing then we can be able to call the API

claims.claim: Cursor-based pagination fetches N+1 items past a stable ID/timestamp cursor (e.g. 11 when you want 10) so the extra item tells you whether more data exists; it's stable against inserts/deletes but can't jump to an arbitrary page, unlike offset pagination.
claims.quote: take 11 items and the reason why we take 11 items

claims.claim: An agent equals model plus harness: the harness is every piece of code, configuration, or execution logic that isn't the model itself — the shared vocabulary for what you're actually optimizing when improving an AI agent.
claims.quote: every piece of code, configuration, or execution logic that isn't the model itself

claims.claim: Prompting quality matters everywhere an agent reads instructions: the system prompt, tool descriptions auto-loaded into context, skill front matter, and sub-agent front matter that specifies when/how to use them.
claims.quote: prompting also applies to like the tool descriptions as well

claims.claim: Add a hook that fires before the agent is allowed to exit, forcing it to recheck its work rather than trusting its own judgment on when it's done.
claims.quote: before the model tries to go and exit, like force it to like recheck the work

claims.claim: Agents are prone to picking the easy way out on verification — testing only trivial cases rather than genuinely hard ones — so harnesses need to explicitly teach them to be thorough.
claims.quote: agents are very susceptible towards like picking the easy way out in verification

claims.claim: Bound a sub-agent's task to roughly 50k–150k (up to 200k) tokens; give it too big a subtask and it drifts into a high-context 'dumb zone' where quality degrades.
claims.quote: I want it to like do things in like a 50k to like a 150k token range, roughly

claims.theme: File system as core harness primitive
claims.claim: The file system is arguably the most foundational harness primitive: agents are already exceptional at using it, it needs no coercion, and it gives the agent persistent storage to offload and later retrieve information outside the context window.
claims.quote: the file system is arguably the most foundational harness primitive

claims.theme: File system as core harness primitive
claims.claim: Models are already exceptional at using file systems, which is why file-system-based context management works with little prompting effort compared to novel tool patterns.
claims.quote: agents are just exceptional at using file systems already

claims.claim: In multi-agent setups, files become the collaboration layer: sub-agents write results to specific files and the main agent reads from them, so decomposed work doesn't pollute the main agent's context window.
claims.quote: file systems actually also become excel- excellent like collaborations places

claims.claim: On a time-bounded terminal-bench run, using max ('X-high') reasoning effort throughout scored only 53.9% (it ran out of time) versus 63.6% at 'high' effort — reasoning quality traded against wall-clock and cost limits.
claims.quote: running only at X high scored 53.9% due to timeouts versus 63.6% at high

claims.claim: Generic public benchmarks are rough vibe checks at best; the real way to measure whether your agent is improving is to build your own representative set of evals/tasks drawn from your actual use case.
claims.quote: the best way to measure problem-solving ability is just to like get a representative set of like evals and tasks like my own bench

claims.theme: Hooks as an underrated harness feature
claims.claim: Hooks/middleware that inject deterministic code execution to control model behavior (not just add tools) are one of the most underrated harness features.
claims.quote: hooks that sort of like control bad model behavior are like really really helpful

claims.claim: The single biggest fix in a bad login screen is color discipline: one accent/CTA color overused across icon, text, outlines, headers, and links divides user attention so nothing stands out — 'if everything is on fire, nothing is on fire.'
claims.quote: if everything is on fire then nothing is on fire

claims.claim: A bright brand/accent color needs to be reserved for primary calls to action and primary areas of concern, not reused everywhere on the screen.
claims.quote: it needs to be reserved for primary calls to action

claims.claim: A text link is invisible as a link if it has no visual difference (uppercase, reduced opacity, underline, or other treatment) from surrounding placeholder/body text.
claims.quote: there is no difference in the treatment of this text to the treatment of the placeholder text

claims.theme: Don't give two CTAs equal weight
claims.claim: Giving a secondary action (e.g. 'Register') the same size and weight as the primary CTA ('Sign In') forces the user to stop and guess which one to click — pick one clear primary action.
claims.quote: I also have an equally weighted equally sized call to action button here to register

claims.claim: A senior-level sign-up form can use no accent color at all — pure black-and-white with strong contrast between placeholder, active, inactive, and link states — and still read as high quality.
claims.quote: very controlled use of color there's actually no color here but that's okay

claims.claim: Fix ambiguous proximity (e.g. a logo lockup that feels loosely attached) by putting the elements in a Figma auto-layout with consistent spacing, or separating them further, so grouping reads intentionally.
claims.quote: put this inside of an auto layout in figma or something like that and give me some consistent spacing

claims.theme: What the best login screens do
claims.claim: Top-tier login screens combine intentional, specific color usage, clear hierarchy, deliberate spacing/layout, and supporting imagery/gradients rather than a blank form.
claims.quote: doing a fantastic job of using Color hierarchy spacing layout bringing in some imagery

claims.theme: Dashboards need a content focal point
claims.claim: In data-heavy dashboards, clear out chrome (big top bars, heavy sidebars) so the actual charts/content — not the logo or nav — become the visual focal point.
claims.quote: we need to clear out the design and allow the information to be the thing that's the focal point

claims.claim: Interface design isn't website design: tools should be simple, easy, straightforward, and sometimes a little boring, rather than optimized for visual excitement.
claims.quote: interface design is not necessarily like web design we are building tools and tools should be simple easy straightforward

claims.theme: Overusing brand color in data viz
claims.claim: Applying the brand color to every pie chart, box, and graph regardless of value makes all data points blend together and lose meaning — data visualization needs its own thoughtful palette, not the brand palette.
claims.quote: there's no reason to use the brand color this much brand color does not have to be used in every pie chart

claims.claim: Senior dashboards strip away most brand color so the content itself (graphs, avatars, flags) does the visual work, keeping branding secondary once the user is inside the tool.
claims.quote: We have Stripped Away a lot of the brand color we don't need it it's not about the brand

claims.claim: Bold neo-brutalist drop shadows can read as senior-level and intentional, but only when reserved for places that need attention (interactive elements, key charts) rather than every element.
claims.quote: these heavy almost Neo brutalism drop Shadows they're thick they're bold they're on purpose

claims.theme: Heavy shadows signal poor contrast skills
claims.claim: Reaching for line separators and heavy drop shadows everywhere is usually a tell that a designer doesn't know how to use color and contrast to create separation.
claims.quote: when somebody doesn't know how to use color and contrast they start to add line separators they start to add too much drop shadow

claims.claim: Red and bright green are 'system colors' reserved for success/error states — using bright red for something like a logout button (not an error) misuses the convention and confuses users.
claims.quote: we usually reserve the colors red and bright green for success and error States these are called System colors

claims.theme: One accent color threaded through the UI
claims.claim: Pick one purposeful accent color (e.g. a punchy blue signaling trust/professionalism for real estate) and thread it consistently through primary, secondary, and tertiary actions rather than scattering multiple colors.
claims.quote: a nice Punchy blue that probably in color theory represents professionalism trustworthiness

claims.claim: Put search/filtering that affects the whole page in the global navigation area at the top; keep filters that only affect a specific section local to that section, so users can predict scope from placement.
claims.quote: we have some of that Global navigation here and what are people doing when they come to Real Estate websites they're probably filtering

claims.claim: You can visually identify a fully AI-designed app because it has a recognizable 'smell' (e.g. odd borders) that distinguishes it from human-tuned design.
claims.quote: you can tell if it's just fully been designed with AI because it has that smell

claims.claim: Building each screen ad hoc without a design system produces visible drift — e.g. one button roundedness on the dashboard and a completely different one in chat within the same app.
claims.quote: there's inconsistency in my app

claims.claim: A design system is a single source of truth for all things design: it contains UI components, design guidelines, and brand identity (colors, copy, etc.).
claims.quote: A design system is a single source of truth for all things design

claims.claim: A design token abstracts a raw design decision into a named variable — e.g. 'padding: 16px' becomes 'padding: spacing-medium' and a hex color becomes 'color: brand-primary.'
claims.quote: the design token would look like padding spacing medium and color brand primary

claims.claim: Global theming tokens make dark mode easy: change the underlying token value once and the update propagates everywhere automatically, instead of hunting down every hardcoded color.
claims.quote: Global theming tokens make it incredibly easy to introduce a dark mode

claims.claim: With tokens, a brand color change doesn't require developers and designers to manually search and replace hex codes across the codebase.
claims.quote: developers and designers do not need to manually search and replace hex codes

claims.claim: Mobin is a design-inspiration platform with onboarding flows, hero sections, and full dashboards you can browse and save by section as raw material before designing.
claims.quote: Mobin has a lot of great examples

claims.theme: Generating a design system from a screenshot
claims.claim: Feed Claude Design a full-page screenshot of an inspiration site with the prompt 'Please create a design system with the attached page. Please do create components using the design system and display the tokens' to get a first-pass design system.
claims.quote: Please create a design system with the attached page

claims.claim: AI-generated design systems aren't meant to be a 1:1 copy of the source screenshot — current AI isn't good at exact replication, but it's good at producing a tunable canvas to build a design system from.
claims.quote: this isn't really onetoone this site and it's not supposed to be like that

claims.claim: Use Claude Design's markup tool to draw directly on the generated output and issue targeted instructions like 'please remove this from the design system' to strip unwanted elements (confetti dots, an AI-looking logo, misaligned badge text).
claims.quote: please remove this from the design system

claims.theme: Public design system as a base
claims.claim: If you lack your own inspiration source, Vercel publishes a public design.md (light and dark) at vercel.com/design.md that can be used as a foundational markdown base to build your own design system from.
claims.quote: verscell.com/design.md they basically have their design system

claims.claim: Letting AI design the entire system with zero personal input makes the product look like everybody else's — always add your own taste/style on top of the AI-generated base.
claims.quote: if you use AI to design the entire thing no sauce or input from you site's going going to look like everybody else's

claims.theme: Porting the design system into a coding agent
claims.claim: After finalizing the design system in Claude Design, sending it to Claude Code (via the 'send to Claude Code' action) lets the coding agent generate a landing page, auth page, and dashboard in one prompt that all follow the same colors, fonts, and spacing without being told to reference the system again.
claims.quote: it followed the colors, it followed the font, it followed the spacing, it followed everything

claims.claim: Because every generated page pulls from one shared design system, fixing a single component issue (e.g. a stray confetti button style) automatically fixes it wherever that component is reused across the app.
claims.quote: because you have a design system, once you fix one thing, it affects the entire thing

disagreements.topic: How much visual personality/decoration a professional UI should carry

positions.position: Interfaces are tools, not brand moments — they should be simple, straightforward, and even a little boring, with decoration and brand color stripped away so content does the talking.

Chooses playful, cartoony-but-tasteful inspiration (family.co) and builds toward hover micro-interactions, emoji explosions, and gradient/liquid-metal button effects as marks of an exceptional, non-generic design.

disagreements.topic: Whether maximum model reasoning effort always improves agent output

positions.position: Under a time-bounded task, running max ('X-high') reasoning throughout scored worse (53.9%) than a 'high' effort setting (63.6%) because it ran out of time — more reasoning is not free and can lose to cost/latency constraints even though it's individually more capable.

gaps: No concrete accessibility guidance (contrast ratios, screen reader patterns, keyboard navigation specifics) beyond a single passing mention of 'optimize for mobile and accessibilities.'
No coverage of responsive/mobile-specific layout patterns or breakpoints for the UI designs critiqued.
No typography guidance beyond token category names (display size, H1/H2/H3) — no advice on font pairing, line height, or reading measure.
No motion/animation design principles (easing curves, durations, when to animate) beyond naming a couple of example micro-interactions (BUI accordion bounce, tilt card).
No discussion of design-to-dev handoff process, versioning of a design system over time, or how teams keep a design system in sync as it evolves post-launch.
No data tying specific design decisions (color, hierarchy, spacing) to measurable outcomes like conversion rate or task completion time — critique in the corpus is qualitative/visual only.
No evaluation or comparison of specific component libraries/CSS frameworks (e.g. Tailwind, shadcn) beyond a single passing name-drop of 'BUI.'
No guidance on how to price, pitch, or present this kind of UI work to clients, despite the corpus repeatedly referencing freelance/agency and portfolio contexts.
